approach_variants.name: Blue Lake Trail to the Y-shaped larch
approach_variants.notes:
From the Blue Lake Trailhead (~5,200 ft) on SR-20 about 1.5 miles west of Washington Pass, walk the maintained trail roughly a mile and a quarter until it opens into a clearing. Leave it at the small stream — often cairned — and follow climbers' tracks up through the slabs alongside the stream into the basin under the west side of the spires.

The meadows here are fragile and heavily used; stay on the established tracks and off the heather.

From the basin, work up the talus toward the west face of South Early Winters Spire, north of the Southwest Couloir.
hazards: fragile alpine meadow crossed by braided tracks — erosion damage and easy to lose the line
shared descent line with South Arete parties, so expect congestion at rappel stations
approach_variants.baseFinding: The base of the route is marked by a larch tree that forks into two trunks in a clear Y — it is the single agreed-upon landmark for this climb and people navigate to it by name. In front of the Y-larch an easy ledge runs up and away from the tree; scramble that ledge and belay off a solid tree, and the first proper pitch follows cracks straight up through an awkward bulge, well protected, to a ledge at the foot of the feature climbers call the Wavy Crack. If you start at a lower or higher point on the rib you skip that first 5.8+ pitch and arrive at the Wavy Crack having missed the best of the lower climbing — so hunt for the Y-larch rather than roping up at whatever looks like the toe. The rib you want is the buttress immediately north of (left of, looking in) the Southwest Couloir.

pitch_detail.notes: Shares the Direct East Buttress's rambling, sometimes-loose first pitch through moss and vegetation to a tree anchor.
A shared crack system with the Direct East Buttress winds through ledges to the base of the large dihedral.
Climbs the shared dihedral through a bulging roof, well protected at the crux move, before easier climbing to a tree ledge.
The last pitch shared with the Direct East Buttress -- a bolt ladder through steep rock -- before Southern Man splits off around halfway up the wall onto its own south-facing headwall.
First headwall pitch: sustained 5.10 finger and hand cracks on excellent rock, with the odd-numbered headwall pitches generally the more straightforward crack climbing.
The route's crux: a short, bulgy face section with bad feet above thin pro; the FA party aided this at 5.9+ C1 in 2008, freed by Bryan Burdo at 5.12a in 2009.
More sustained 5.10 crack climbing continues up the headwall with the same excellent finger locks found on the pitch below.
A harder, cruxier face-climbing pitch linking crack systems; belays on this upper section are reported as vague and unfixed, so build gear anchors with care.
The final headwall pitch eases to sustained but comfortable 5.10- crack climbing, topping out near the summit and the standard South Arete descent.

waypoints.name: Blue Lake Trailhead, Hwy 20
waypoints.note: Northwest Forest Pass required to park; many East Buttress parties instead park at the unmarked hairpin-curve pullout ~1 mi east on Hwy 20 to shortcut into Spire Gully.
waypoints.directions: Drive Highway 20 to the Blue Lake Trailhead, about 1.5 miles west of Washington Pass, and park in the small lot; a Northwest Forest Pass is required. Many East Buttress parties instead carry on east toward Washington Pass and park at the unmarked 180-degree hairpin pullout roughly a mile along, below the east faces of the spires, which drops you straight into the bottom of Spire Gully. The standard descent comes back out at Blue Lake, so if you leave the car at the hairpin, plan on a shuttle or a hitch along the highway to close the loop.

waypoints.name: Hairpin-curve pullout on Hwy 20
waypoints.note: Alternate, more direct start used by most East Buttress parties: park at the 180-degree hairpin turn just below Washington Pass and hike straight up into Spire Gully instead of via the Blue Lake trail.
waypoints.directions: This is an alternate roadside start rather than somewhere you walk to from the Blue Lake lot: parties using it drive back east along the highway toward Washington Pass and park at the big 180-degree hairpin below the spires, which puts them straight into the bottom of Spire Gully. It cuts out the traverse in from the Blue Lake trail on the way up. The standard descent comes back out at Blue Lake, though, so plan on a shuttle or a hitch along the highway to close the loop.

waypoints.name: Spire Gully, last large tree
waypoints.note: Follow occasional cairns up the open gully below the NEWS/SEWS col to the last large tree standing in its center — the cue to angle out of the gully here.
waypoints.directions: From the hairpin climb straight up and southwest into the open gully below the col between the two spires, following the occasional cairns. The whole line is visible from the road, so pick it out before you start walking. Follow the gully to the last big tree standing in the middle of it — that tree is the cue to stop going straight up.

waypoints.name: Talus traverse to NEWS-SEWS notch gully
waypoints.note: From the last tree, traverse right across talus (snow early season, crampons/axe recommended) into the gully leading up to the deep cleft separating North and South Early Winters Spire.
waypoints.directions: Leave the gully at the tree and traverse right across talus into the gully that runs up to the deep cleft between North and South Early Winters Spire. Early in the season this traverse is snow rather than talus and is worth an axe and crampons; later it is loose blocky footing.

waypoints.name: NEWS-SEWS notch
waypoints.note: Gain the notch between the two spires, then traverse left (south) below South Early Winters Spire's east face to reach the buttress base.
waypoints.directions: Follow that gully up to the notch. It steepens and gets looser toward the top and holds snow late into the summer, so keep the party out of each other's fall line rather than climbing directly above one another.

waypoints.name: Base of East Buttress
waypoints.note: Rope up here; the Direct East Buttress climbs ~9 pitches of 5.8-5.9 crack-and-face up the buttress crest to the summit.
waypoints.directions: From the notch traverse left, southward, along ledges beneath the east face until you are under the crest of the buttress. It is only a short way along and barely above the notch, so treat it as a traverse rather than a climb, and rope up once you are there.

waypoints.name: South Early Winters Spire summit
waypoints.note: Highest summit of the Liberty Bell group; sweeping views of Liberty Bell, the Wine Spires, and North Early Winters Spire across the notch.
waypoints.directions: The standard line takes the easier lower-angle rock up the toe of the buttress rather than the steep dihedral system the Direct start uses, then follows cracks and broken ledges up the crest on clean granite, with the sustained crack-and-corner crux about a third of the way up. Higher pitches ease off and merge with the Direct's terrain, and the short final pitch to the top is often simul-climbed.

waypoints.name: South Arete downclimb/rappels
waypoints.note: Standard descent: downclimb the South Arete (mostly 3rd/4th class with a short exposed 5th-class step), then three single-rope raps from bolted anchors to the base before dropping back toward Blue Lake trail or hitching from the hairpin.
waypoints.directions: Do not reverse the buttress. The way off is the South Arete: mostly third and fourth class downclimbing with one short exposed fifth-class step, then three single-rope rappels from bolted anchors to the base. From there drop back toward the Blue Lake trail, or back into Spire Gully if a car was left at the hairpin.

before.descent_text: The documented lower pitches (P1 to a fixed 2-bolt anchor, P2 to ledges) suggest Free Mojo can be descended with rappels using a 60m rope from the fixed anchors if not continuing to the top — a party retreating after pitch 2 would rappel P2 then P1 back to the ground. For the full route to the summit (6 pitches), finish via the standard South Arete descent: downclimb the arete to the Rabbit Ears, then 3 single-rope rappels (60m) from bolted anchors/chains down the gully to the base.

before.approach: Start at the Blue Lake Trailhead (elev. ~5,200 ft) on SR-20 just west of Washington Pass. Follow the well-built Blue Lake Trail (Trail #314) as it climbs gently through subalpine fir and larch forest, switchbacking up open slabs with good views back at the highway. After roughly 1.3-1.5 miles and about 1,000 ft of gain, watch for a minor stream crossing/drainage coming down from the basin below the Early Winter Spires — this is well before Blue Lake itself, which lies another mile-plus further on the maintained trail. Leave the maintained trail here and pick up the climbers' boot path (cairned but braided in spots) that works up through granite slabs and heather benches, then continues up open talus and boulder country roughly parallel to the stream, which is a reliable water source through most of the season lower down but disappears into talus higher up — fill up before leaving it. Continue up this climbers' trail, angling toward the southwestern corner/toe of South Early Winter Spire (the right-hand, southernmost of the two spires, before the saddle). Expect roughly 2,000 ft of gain from where you leave the maintained trail to reach the base of the route at the level of the North/South spire saddle, for a total of about 2.5 hours and up to ~2,000 ft of gain from the car. The path is mostly straightforward but loses definition on the upper talus and slab benches — trend toward the obvious southwest corner of the spire rather than chasing any single cairn line, and take care on the granite slabs low down when wet or covered in old snow, which can persist into early summer in shaded gullies.

approach_variants.name: Blue Lake Trail to the southwest toe of the spire
approach_variants.notes:
From the Blue Lake Trailhead (~5,200 ft) on SR-20 about 1.5 miles west of Washington Pass, follow the maintained trail as it climbs through fir and larch and out onto open slabs. After roughly a mile and a quarter to a mile and a half the ground opens up and the Liberty Bell-Concord-Early Winters skyline comes into view; the climbers' track leaves the maintained trail here, at a minor stream draining the basin, sometimes marked with a cairn. This is well short of Blue Lake itself, which is another mile-plus along the maintained trail — if you reach the lake you have gone too far.

The climbers' path works up through granite slabs and heather benches and then up open talus roughly parallel to the stream. The stream is good water low down and vanishes into the talus higher up, so fill there.

Higher, the path loses definition on the talus and slab benches and braids. Rather than chasing one cairn line, navigate to the feature: the southwest corner at the end of the ridge on the right.
hazards: wet or snow-covered granite slabs low on the climbers' path
braided path and loss of definition on the upper talus
old snow persisting in shaded gullies into early summer
queueing at rappel stations on busy weekends, since this is also the descent line for other routes
approach_variants.baseFinding: You are aiming for the southwest corner — the toe where the south ridge of South Early Winters Spire runs down and ends, which is the right-hand (southernmost) of the two spires, reached before the saddle between them. The arete itself is broad and broken rather than a knife edge, and it separates the Southwest Couloir on its left from the steep East Face on its right; standing at the base you should have the couloir up to one side and steep unclimbable-looking wall to the other. The first pitch begins with a short steep crack; above it you either go right and up across a slab at 5.5 to a small tree, or left across a short friction slab at 5.5. If you are stood at the bottom of a broad snow or scree gully with nothing to climb, you have drifted into the Southwest Couloir and need to move right onto the ridge toe. If you are under steep continuous rock, you have gone too far right onto the east side.

approach_variants.name: Early-season, snow in the basin
approach_variants.notes:
The same line in from Blue Lake, but with the basin under snow the climbers' path through the slabs and talus is buried and you are navigating by terrain rather than by boot track. Firm morning snow makes the ascent quicker than summer talus; softening afternoon snow makes the descent slower.

SR-20 across Washington Pass is gated every winter, typically from late November or early December until mid-April to early May, so the season begins when the highway does.
hazards: moat at the base where snow pulls off the rock
firm snow in the couloir requiring axe and possibly crampons
buried climbers' path — navigate by the couloir and ridge toe, not by cairns
approach_variants.baseFinding: With snow filling the basin the Southwest Couloir is a clean white line and the arete is the rock rib on its right-hand side — that contrast actually makes the toe EASIER to identify than in summer, when couloir and ridge are both grey. Walk up the snow of the couloir's edge and step right onto the rock at the ridge toe, where the short steep crack of the first pitch starts. Expect a moat at the snow-rock junction. Take an axe: the alternative descent down the couloir holds firm snow well into summer.
